title: Gaia and the New Politics of Love: Notes for a Poly Planet
author: Serena Anderlini-D'Onofrio
target_audience: Readers interested in polyamory and alternative relationship models
Scholars and students of gender, sexuality, and LGBTQ+ studies
Activists seeking intersections between love, politics, and sustainability
core_themes: The connection between ecological awareness and polyamorous relationship models
Challenging monogamy as a socio-cultural norm
Inclusivity, diversity, and fluidity in love and intimacy
Gaia theory as a metaphor for social and relational interconnectedness
The intersection of environmental, sexual, and political liberation
Sustainable love: parallels between planetary health and human relationships
primary_purpose: To explore how embracing polyamory and pluralistic models of love can foster a more sustainable, inclusive, and resilient global society—drawing inspiration from Gaia theory and connecting ecological wisdom to new forms of loving and relating.

structure_format.narrative_style: Philosophical, interdisciplinary, reflective, weaving personal narrative with theoretical analysis
structure_format.organization: Divided into thematic chapters blending memoir, critique, academic theory, and advocacy; uses notes and essays-style reflections
features: References to ecology, gender, and queer theory
Calls to activism and new paradigms

key_concepts_lessons: Monogamy is a cultural construct, not a biological or ecological necessity.
Polyamory mirrors the interconnected, adaptive systems of Gaia; diversity in relationships parallels biodiversity.
Expanding concepts of love and family can help society better address ecological and social crises.
Intimacy, openness, and inclusivity in relationships foster resilience both in people and in planetary systems.
Challenging patriarchal, heteronormative norms can liberate personal and collective capacity for love.
Planetary health (Gaia) and personal/interpersonal health are deeply intertwined.
notable_features: Blends ecological theory (Gaia) with concepts of polyamory
Combines academic language with accessible, personal narrative
Advocates for intersectionality in activism, love, and ecological stewardship
Early, influential work in both eco-sexuality and polyamory literature
cultural_historical_context: Written during a period of growing interest in alternative relationship models, climate change, and social justice movements, the book situates polyamory within the broader context of ecological crisis and sexual liberation, responding to early 21st century calls for radical change in both love and society.
reception_impact: Praised for its originality, interdisciplinary reach, and visionary synthesis
Influential in the eco-sexuality and polyamory communities
Used in courses on gender, sexuality, and environmental studies
Some critics find its style dense or its vision utopian, but others cite its unique contribution to both sexuality and ecological thought
comparable_titles: Sex Ecology Spirituality by Ken Wilber
The Ethical Slut by Dossie Easton and Janet W. Hardy
Gaia: A New Look at Life on Earth by James Lovelock
Polyamory in the 21st Century by Deborah Anapol
